quests.scene: You're emailing your professor to ask for a two-day extension on an essay because you were ill this week.
options: Hi Prof, any chance I could get a couple more days? Been sick lol.
I need an extension on the essay. I was ill this week, so two days please.
I was wondering if perhaps it might be conceivable to ask about a little more time, if that isn't too much trouble at all?
Dear Professor Lin, I'm sorry to ask, but could I have a two-day extension? I've been unwell this week.
quests.hint: Formal, direct, and brief: not chatty, not commanding, not over-apologetic.
quests.explanation: The correct email is polite and specific without groveling. The casual version is too informal for a professor, the blunt one sounds like a demand, and the hedged one buries the request.
quests.culturalNote: Academic emails generally stay formal and get to the point quickly.

quests.instruction: Pick the response that fits the relationship.
quests.scene: You're texting a close friend to ask if you can borrow twenty pounds until Friday.
options: Dear Jo, I would be most grateful if you could lend me twenty pounds until Friday.
I'm a bit short this week, hope things are okay with you though?
Hey, could I borrow £20 till Friday? I'll pay you back then.
Send me £20 and I'll pay you back, you know I'm good for it.
quests.hint: Match the register you normally use with this friend.
quests.explanation: A clear, casual request with a date fits a close friendship. Too formal sounds odd, hinting is unclear, and pushing assumes too much.
quests.culturalNote: Money requests between friends work best when clear and time-bound.

quests.instruction: What is the most tactful response?
quests.scene: In a quiet carriage on a train, a man is loudly talking on his phone. You'd like him to stop.
options: Sorry to interrupt — would you mind taking your call outside the quiet carriage?
Could you be quiet? This is the quiet carriage, in case you hadn't noticed.
Um, sorry, I don't want to be a bother, but maybe, possibly, if it's okay...
Excuse me, phones aren't allowed in here at all, you know.
quests.hint: Be clear about the request without lecturing.
quests.explanation: A polite, specific request gives him an easy fix. Sarcasm, excessive hedging, or overstating the rule invite argument or confusion.
quests.culturalNote: Quiet carriages have clear norms, but an unsolicited lecture rarely helps.

quests.instruction: Choose the most constructive way to say this.
quests.scene: A colleague's presentation had a wrong number on slide six. You want to tell her privately before the client meeting.
options: Slide six was wrong. You need to fix it before the client sees it tomorrow, and please check the other slides too while you're at it.
It was mostly fine, maybe have another look at some of it later.
The presentation was strong overall. Could we check slide six's figures together? I think one number's off.
By the way, everyone noticed the wrong number on slide six.
quests.hint: Be specific about the problem, and not harsh or vague.
quests.explanation: Naming the exact slide and offering to check together protects her dignity. Bluntness, vagueness, or mentioning others' reactions either sting or don't solve anything.
quests.culturalNote: Private, specific feedback is far more effective than general or public criticism.

quests.scene: A friend proudly shows you her dramatic new haircut and asks, 'Do you like it?' You're not sure you do.
options: It's a big change — it'll take me a minute to get used to, but the color suits you.
I preferred the old one, if I'm being truthful with you. It suited your face better, and this looks a bit severe.
It's fine.
Wow, that's a brave choice, isn't it?
quests.hint: Be honest without being harsh: find something true and kind.
quests.explanation: Naming the change and one real positive is honest and kind. Blunt truth, flat replies, and backhanded compliments all hurt.
quests.culturalNote: Tactful honesty is valued, especially about appearance.

quests.scene: A coworker asks you to review a forty-page document by tomorrow. You can't do all of it, but you could help with part.
options: I'm so sorry, I'm really busy, you know how it is around here lately.
I can't do a full review by tomorrow, but I can look at the summary section tonight.
Tomorrow isn't realistic at all. You should have asked me a lot earlier than this, because I have my own deadlines to meet as well.
I'd love to help but I just can't, sorry, maybe someone else can.
quests.hint: Give a clear limit and say what you can do.
quests.explanation: Stating what you can offer keeps the relationship helpful. Vague apologies, blame, or plain refusal leave your coworker without options.
quests.culturalNote: In workplaces, offering a partial alternative is often better than a flat no.

quests.scene: A friend keeps asking how much you earn. You're not comfortable sharing.
options: That's none of your business, and I'd like you to stop asking me about it every time we see each other, please.
Oh, it's okay, I suppose. Enough to get by on, really, nothing special.
I'd rather not talk about what I earn — but I'm happy to talk about the job itself.
Why do you keep asking about money all the time?
quests.hint: Set the limit and open a different door.
quests.explanation: Stating your limit kindly and offering another topic protects both privacy and friendship. Harsh refusal or deflecting answers don't settle it.
quests.culturalNote: Attitudes toward discussing pay vary widely; stating a personal boundary is acceptable.

quests.scene: Your manager messages you at 10 p.m. asking for a file. It can easily wait until morning.
options: Please don't message me after work hours, it's not fair to ask.
Sure, I'm working on it now, and I'll send it over in a bit.
I'm not on the clock right now, so this will have to wait.
I saw this late — I'll pick it up first thing tomorrow morning.
quests.hint: Set the limit through what you'll do, not what she shouldn't.
quests.explanation: Stating when you'll act sets a boundary without confrontation. Demanding rules, giving in, or announcing you're off-duty can sound combative.
quests.culturalNote: Norms about after-hours contact differ; a clear timeframe avoids conflict.

quests.scene: At a family dinner, an aunt asks whether you and your partner plan to have children. You'd rather not discuss it.
options: I'd rather keep that private for now, but thanks for asking. How's your garden coming along?
Why does everyone keep asking me that at family events?
We'll see, maybe someday, who knows what will happen.
That's really not an appropriate question to ask at dinner, and I'm surprised you would bring it up in front of everybody here.
quests.hint: Decline the topic warmly and change the subject.
quests.explanation: A gentle limit plus a new topic keeps the mood warm. Complaining or scolding creates tension, and vague answers invite more questions.
quests.culturalNote: Questions about family plans can feel intrusive; redirecting kindly often works.

quests.scene: A colleague keeps interrupting you in meetings. You want to make your point.
options: Could you stop interrupting me? It's really rude, you know, and you've done it three times in this meeting alone already.
I'd like to finish my point — could I have a minute before we discuss it?
Sorry, I'm probably talking too much, please go ahead.
It's fine, speak, I really don't mind if you go first.
quests.hint: Reclaim the floor politely but firmly.
quests.explanation: Stating what you need in a neutral way protects your point. Accusations or giving way leave you unheard.
quests.culturalNote: Assertive but neutral language works well when interrupted in meetings.

quests.scene: You want to raise the issue of your pay with your manager after taking on client accounts this year.
options: I think I deserve more money than I'm getting right now.
I'd like to discuss my pay — I've taken on the client accounts this year.
Would there ever be a chance of some sort of raise at some point?
Everyone else got a raise, so I would like one too.
quests.hint: Bring evidence and be direct about the topic.
quests.explanation: Naming the request and the reason makes a business case. Feelings, vagueness, or comparisons make it easier to dismiss.
quests.culturalNote: Salary conversations are stronger when tied to concrete contributions.

quests.scene: A customer emails angrily about a late order. It has shipped today and you can upgrade delivery for free.
options: I'm sorry for the delay. Your order shipped today, and I've upgraded it to express at no cost.
Delays happen due to factors outside our control, as clearly stated in our shipping policy, which is linked on our website for your convenience.
We understand you're frustrated, but the delay wasn't really our fault.
Sorry about that! Hope it arrives soon, fingers crossed for you.
quests.hint: Apologize, give facts, and fix what you can.
quests.explanation: Apology plus a concrete fix resolves frustration. Quoting policy, blaming others, or casual hopes don't address the problem.
quests.culturalNote: Customers often care more about a concrete solution than an explanation.

quests.scene: You're meeting your friend's grandmother, Mrs. Alvarez, for the first time at a family lunch.
options: Hey Mrs. A! Great to meet you, I've heard so much!
It's lovely to meet you, Mrs. Alvarez.
Hello, Alvarez. Good to meet you at last.
Nice to finally meet you, Rosa. I love your home.
quests.hint: Use the address that shows respect until invited otherwise.
quests.explanation: Using her title is respectful for a first meeting with an older person. Nicknames, surnames alone, or first names assume too much.
quests.culturalNote: Many families appreciate titles until an older relative invites first names.

quests.scene: You're texting your landlord, Mr. Peters, about a heater that stopped working yesterday.
options: Heater's broken. When are you fixing it?
Hi, sorry to bother you, it's probably nothing, but the heater seems slightly off maybe?
Hi Mr. Peters, the heater in the living room stopped working yesterday. Could someone take a look this week?
The heater is broken and it's freezing. Please fix this immediately.
quests.hint: Be clear about the problem and what you're asking for.
quests.explanation: Specifics plus a polite request give him what he needs. Blunt demands, over-apologetic hedging, or urgency without details are less effective.
quests.culturalNote: Written maintenance requests are best when specific and courteous.

quests.scene: Your team gathers to celebrate your manager Sarah's promotion, and you say a few words.
options: Congratulations, Sarah — well deserved. We're lucky to have you leading us.
Congrats! Don't forget us little people now, will you?
Well done. I suppose you deserve it after all this time.
Congratulations on your accomplishment. We wish you every success.
quests.hint: Warm, sincere, and appropriate for a boss.
quests.explanation: Sincere praise with a personal touch fits the moment. Teasing, backhanded compliments, or stiff formality miss the warmth.
quests.culturalNote: Congratulating a manager works best when sincere and not overly familiar.

quests.scene: A friend invited you to her wedding, but the travel cost is too high for you.
options: Thank you so much for inviting me. I can't make the trip, but I'll be thinking of you both that day.
I can't afford it, sorry, weddings are just so expensive these days, with the flights, the hotel, the outfit and the gift on top of everything else.
I'll try to come, but it looks unlikely at the moment.
That's very far away. Why not marry somewhere closer?
quests.hint: Be honest about the no and warm about the invitation.
quests.explanation: A clear, kind no with warm wishes respects the friendship. Vague maybes or complaints about the location hurt.
quests.culturalNote: Declining a wedding invite is more gracious with prompt and warm honesty.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: A neighbor invites you for drinks again. You like her, but you want to keep the evening short.
options: I can't, I'm busy, sorry, maybe another time perhaps.
Sure, I'll stay as long as you like, no rush at all.
I don't really enjoy these evenings very much, to be honest.
Thanks, I'd love a quick one, but I'll need to leave by eight.
quests.hint: Accept warmly and state your limit up front.
quests.explanation: Accepting with a time limit makes the boundary clear from the start. Refusing outright or accepting without limits leads to awkwardness later.
quests.culturalNote: Stating a time limit early is easier than leaving abruptly.

quests.scene: A colleague asks you to join a charity run, but running isn't something you'd enjoy.
options: It's a great cause, but running isn't for me. I'd be happy to donate instead.
I hate running. Count me out, sorry, it's not for me.
Maybe next year, I'll think about it and let you know closer to the date, once I see how the rest of the year looks for me.
I already do enough for charity throughout the year.
quests.hint: Decline the activity, not the cause.
quests.explanation: Supporting the cause differently shows you care. Bluntness, false maybes, or defensiveness make it feel like a rejection.
quests.culturalNote: Offering an alternative support option is a common polite way to decline.

quests.scene: A friend texts 'where r u??' as you're running late. You're stuck on a delayed train, twenty minutes away.
options: Chill, I'm coming, I'll be there soon enough, don't worry about it so much, it's not like we have a booking or anything anyway.
Sorry, I'm stuck on the train — twenty minutes away. I'll text when I'm close.
I'll be there when I get there, no need to keep asking.
On my way!! Almost there, just a few minutes more!
quests.hint: Give accurate information and keep it warm.
quests.explanation: Honest timing and a plan let her adjust. Impatience or false reassurance makes it worse.
quests.culturalNote: Accurate updates avoid resentment better than vague reassurance.

quests.scene: You've been copied on an email thread that has nothing to do with your work.
options: Stop adding me to your emails, this isn't my area at all.
Not sure why I'm CC'd on this, it doesn't concern me.
Remove me from this thread please, I've got no need for it at all and my inbox is already full of messages that have nothing to do with me.
Hi all — could you please remove me from this thread? I think I was added by mistake.
quests.hint: State the problem neutrally and ask for the fix.
quests.explanation: A polite request with a possible explanation avoids blame. Sharper wording sounds annoyed or dismissive.
quests.culturalNote: Email etiquette assumes the mistake was accidental unless shown otherwise.

quests.scene: A coworker forwards you a joke email you find inappropriate for work.
options: This is offensive; I'm going to report you to HR about it.
Ha, funny one. Maybe don't send them to everyone though.
I'd rather not get jokes like this at work — no offense meant.
Please don't send me stuff like this anymore, it's awkward.
quests.hint: State your preference without escalating.
quests.explanation: A polite, low-key limit keeps the relationship intact. Threatening or joking about it can either escalate or muddy the message.
quests.culturalNote: Workplace norms vary, but a calm early limit often prevents bigger problems.

quests.scene: A friend asks for your opinion on her business plan. You like the idea but worry about the costs.
options: It's a great plan, go for it, I'm sure it will all work out!
I don't think it'll work, so I'd think twice about it before you put any of your savings into the business, if I were you.
I'm not the right person to ask about business, sorry.
I like the idea, but I'm worried about the costs — could we go through the numbers together?
quests.hint: Praise what's real and raise the concern specifically.
quests.explanation: Naming a strength and a concrete worry, with an offer to help, is honest and supportive. False encouragement or bluntness doesn't help her decide.
quests.culturalNote: Constructive honesty helps friends more than flattery.

quests.scene: In a queue at the post office, the person behind you is standing very close and it's making you uncomfortable.
options: You're standing way too close to me, you know that?
Ugh, back off a bit, will you? It's really uncomfortable.
Sorry, could you give me a little more room?
Excuse me. Some space, please, thanks.
quests.hint: Ask calmly for what you need.
quests.explanation: A polite request gives them a simple way to fix it. Accusations or curt commands can make it a confrontation.
quests.culturalNote: Comfortable personal distance varies, so a polite request is usually all that's needed.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: A friend has borrowed your jacket for three weeks and hasn't returned it. You need it for next week.
options: You never return anything, do you? It's happened before.
It's okay, keep it, I probably won't need it that much.
I'm starting to think you're keeping it on purpose.
I need my jacket back this week — can you bring it on Friday?
quests.hint: State the need and a specific time.
quests.explanation: A clear request with a day is easy to act on. Accusations or brushing it off won't get the jacket back.
quests.culturalNote: Specific requests make it easier for friends to follow through.

quests.scene: In a team meeting, your manager announces a plan you think is risky. You'd like to raise it respectfully.
options: I see it differently — could I share another option after the meeting?
That won't work, and I can prove it if you give me a moment.
You're the boss; I'll do whatever you decide, no problem.
With respect, I think this idea is flawed and should be reconsidered.
quests.hint: Disagree without challenging her in front of everyone.
quests.explanation: Offering to discuss later keeps the disagreement constructive and private. Public contradiction or silent compliance both cost you something.
quests.culturalNote: Hierarchies often prefer disagreement handled privately rather than in front of the team.

quests.scene: You want a senior leader's advice on a project decision, and you've never spoken to her before.
options: Can I pick your brain sometime? It's about a project.
I'd value your advice on a project decision. Would you have twenty minutes this week?
Could you spare a little time sometime? Only if you're not busy, of course, and only if it isn't any trouble at all for you, please!
I need your help with my project, when are you free?
quests.hint: Be specific about the ask and respectful of her time.
quests.explanation: A clear request with a time frame respects her schedule. Vague or over-apologetic requests are harder to say yes to.
quests.culturalNote: Senior colleagues generally appreciate concise, specific requests.

quests.scene: Your manager gives feedback with which you partly disagree. You accept the timing point but want to explain the budget.
options: I disagree with your feedback, and I think it's unfair, because I worked really hard on this project and nobody appreciated it, including you.
Okay, I'll fix it. I probably did it wrong all along.
You don't understand how complicated the budget was.
Thanks for the feedback. I see your point on the timing, though I'd like to explain my reasoning on the budget.
quests.hint: Acknowledge what's valid, then explain the rest.
quests.explanation: Accepting part and explaining the rest keeps the conversation professional. Flat disagreement or self-blame doesn't move it forward.
quests.culturalNote: Receiving feedback well includes separating what you accept from what you'd like to discuss.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: A friend is often late and you end up waiting alone. You'd like to raise it kindly.
options: You're always late and I'm sick of waiting for you.
It's fine, I don't really mind waiting for you at all.
When you're late, I end up waiting half an hour. Could you text if you're running behind?
Maybe we should meet closer to where you live instead, so you don't have any excuse to be late again, and I won't have to wait around by myself.
quests.hint: Describe the effect and suggest a simple fix.
quests.explanation: Describing the impact and offering a small fix invites cooperation. Blaming or hiding your feelings leaves the problem in place.
quests.culturalNote: Framing a request around a specific behavior is less likely to sound like an attack.

quests.scene: Your landlord says he'll be dropping by your flat next week without saying when.
options: You can't just come in whenever you like, that's not allowed, and I'll speak to a tenants' advice service if you keep trying it on.
I'd prefer notice before any visit — could you give me 24 hours so I can be home?
Sure, come in any time, it's your flat after all.
I'll think about it and get back to you sometime.
quests.hint: State your need and a specific request.
quests.explanation: Naming the notice you need is clear and respectful. Legal threats, giving in, or stalling all cause problems later.
quests.culturalNote: Tenant rights differ by place, but polite requests for notice are commonly accepted.

quests.scene: A buyer on an online marketplace asks for your home address to collect an item.
options: Why do you need my address? That sounds suspicious to me.
I'd rather not share my address — could we meet somewhere public?
Sure, it's 12 Elm Road, come any time this weekend.
I don't feel comfortable with that, sorry, so no.
quests.hint: Protect your privacy but keep the deal alive.
quests.explanation: Offering a public meeting keeps the sale possible while protecting you. Accusing, complying, or a flat refusal lose either safety or the sale.
quests.culturalNote: Meeting in public places is widely recommended for marketplace transactions.
